title: Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog

toc.title: 4.1 Plasmodium: habitat, structure, life cycle and types of malaria
4.2 Earthworm (Pheretima): morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance
4.3 Frog (Rana): morphology, body systems and physiology

html:
Study of Selected Animals carries 6 of the 40 Zoology questions — more than any other single chapter outside Human Biology.

Three type animals are named: the malarial parasite Plasmodium (habitat, structure, life cycle and the types of malaria), the earthworm Pheretima posthuma (morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance) and the frog Rana tigrina (morphology, body systems and physiology).

Expect about two questions on each, almost all of them numbers and names: which segment, which stage, which host, which species, which chamber.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Plasmodium: female Anopheles is the definitive host (sexual phase), man the intermediate host (asexual schizogony); sporozoite infects man, gametocytes infect the mosquito.
  • The stages in order — liver schizogony → erythrocytic (Golgi) cycle → gametocytes → gametes in the mosquito stomach → zygote (the only diploid stage) → ookinete → oocyst on the stomach wall → sporozoites → salivary glands.
  • The four classic species with their fever intervals: P. vivax benign tertian (48 h, relapses from hypnozoites), P. falciparum malignant tertian (cerebral malaria), P. malariae quartan (72 h), P. ovale ovale tertian.
  • Earthworm segment numbers: clitellum 14–16, female pore 14, male pores 18, genital papillae 17 and 19, spermathecal pores 5/6–8/9, testes 10–11, ovaries 13, gizzard 8–9, stomach 9–14, caeca 26, hearts 7, 9, 12, 13.
  • Earthworm physiology: haemoglobin dissolved in plasma, closed circulation, cutaneous respiration, three kinds of nephridia, protandrous hermaphrodite with cross-fertilisation in the cocoon.
  • Frog: three ways of breathing, buccal force pump, three-chambered heart with sinus venosus (pacemaker) and spiral valve, nucleated RBCs, mesonephric kidneys, urinogenital duct in the male, 10 pairs of cranial nerves, external fertilisation and thyroxine-controlled metamorphosis.

4.1 Plasmodium: habitat, structure, life cycle and types of malaria

Systematic position and habitat

Rank Taxon
Kingdom Protista
Phylum Protozoa (Apicomplexa)
Class Sporozoa — no locomotory organelles, all parasitic, spore-forming
Genus Plasmodium

Plasmodium is an intracellular, digenetic (two-host) parasite.

Host Status Where the parasite lives Phase
Man intermediate (secondary) host liver cells (hepatocytes) and red blood cells asexual — schizogony; gametocytes formed
Female Anopheles mosquito definitive (primary) host and vector stomach (midgut) wall, haemocoel and salivary glands sexual — gamogony, fertilisation, sporogony

Only the female Anopheles transmits malaria: the male feeds on plant juices, while the female needs a blood meal to mature her eggs.

Structure of the stages

Stage Structure Where
Sporozoite slender, sickle- (spindle-) shaped, about 10–15 μm; one central nucleus; pellicle with microtubules; apical complex (polar ring, rhoptries, micronemes) for entering cells; glides, no cilia or flagella salivary glands of mosquito → injected into man; the infective stage for man
Cryptozoite / schizont large multinucleate body formed in a liver cell liver
Merozoite small, oval, uninucleate; invades a fresh RBC liver and blood
Trophozoite feeding stage in the RBC; first a signet-ring (ring stage, a large vacuole with the nucleus at one side), then amoeboid; digests haemoglobin, leaving the brown pigment haemozoin RBC
Erythrocytic schizont multinucleate stage that divides into merozoites RBC
Gametocytes microgametocyte (male, smaller) and macrogametocyte (female, larger); round in P. vivax, crescent-shaped in P. falciparum RBC; the infective stage for the mosquito
Microgametes / macrogamete 4–8 slender flagellated microgametes from one microgametocyte (exflagellation); one macrogamete from each macrogametocyte mosquito stomach
Zygote → ookinete diploid zygote becomes a motile, worm-like ookinete mosquito stomach
Oocyst rounded cyst on the outer surface of the stomach wall mosquito stomach wall

The life cycle

A. In man — asexual phase (schizogony)

  1. Infection. A female Anopheles injects sporozoites with her saliva. Within about half an hour they leave the blood and enter liver cells.
  2. Pre-erythrocytic schizogony (liver). Each sporozoite grows into a schizont that divides into thousands of merozoites (cryptomerozoites); the liver cell bursts and they enter the blood. In P. vivax and P. ovale some sporozoites become dormant hypnozoites, which wake weeks or months later and cause relapses. (Older books describe a secondary liver cycle, the exo-erythrocytic schizogony; relapses are now explained by the hypnozoites.)
  3. Erythrocytic schizogony — the Golgi cycle. A merozoite enters an RBC → ring trophozoite → amoeboid trophozoite, eating haemoglobin → schizont → 12–24 merozoites (P. vivax). The RBCs burst together, releasing merozoites, cell debris and haemozoin into the plasma; this causes the paroxysm of fever. The merozoites attack fresh RBCs and the cycle repeats every 48 h in P. vivax.
  4. Gametogony. After several cycles some merozoites develop into gametocytes inside RBCs. They do not divide further in man; they wait to be sucked up by a mosquito.

The time from the bite to the first parasites in the blood is the prepatent period; to the first fever, the incubation period — usually about two weeks (12–17 days) for P. vivax.

B. In the female Anopheles — sexual phase

  1. Gamogony (in the stomach, within minutes of the blood meal): the microgametocyte throws out 4–8 flagellated microgametes (exflagellation); the macrogametocyte matures into one macrogamete. All other blood stages are digested.
  2. Fertilisation (anisogamy) gives a zygote (synkaryon) — the only diploid stage — which becomes the motile, vermiform ookinete.
  3. The ookinete bores through the stomach wall and rounds up beneath its outer lining as an oocyst.
  4. Sporogony: the first division in the oocyst is meiosis, so all later stages are haploid; repeated divisions give thousands of sporozoites. The oocyst bursts, sporozoites drift through the haemocoel and collect in the salivary glands, ready for the next bite. Sporogony takes about 10–14 days and stops in cold weather — one reason malaria is a disease of the warm Terai and not of the high hills.
Hosts and phases — the commonest reversal

The definitive host is the one in which sexual reproduction (fertilisation) happens — the mosquito. Man, in whom only asexual multiplication occurs, is the intermediate host, however much he suffers.

And the mosquito does not catch the infection from sporozoites: it needs gametocytes in the blood it sucks.

The malarial fever

The paroxysm has three stages: a cold stage (shivering, 15–60 min), a hot stage (fever up to 40–41 °C, 2–6 h) and a sweating stage (2–4 h), after which the patient feels well until the next batch of RBCs bursts.

Repeated destruction of RBCs causes anaemia and an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly). The fever is caused by haemozoin and other toxins released when the RBCs rupture.

Types of malaria

Species Malaria Erythrocytic cycle (fever) Distinctive points
P. vivax benign tertian 48 h — fever every third day commonest in Nepal and South Asia; infected RBCs enlarged with Schüffner's dots; hypnozoites → relapse
P. falciparum malignant tertian (subtertian, pernicious) 36–48 h, irregular most dangerous; invades RBCs of all ages, so parasite counts soar; crescent-shaped gametocytes; sticky infected RBCs block brain capillaries → cerebral malaria; blackwater fever (haemoglobin in urine); no hypnozoites
P. malariae quartan 72 h — fever every fourth day mild but long-lasting; band-shaped trophozoites
P. ovale ovale (mild) tertian 48 h rare, mainly tropical Africa; oval infected RBCs; hypnozoites → relapse
P. knowlesi quotidian 24 h monkey malaria of South-East Asia that can infect man

Discovery. Charles Laveran (1880) saw the parasite in human blood; Camillo Golgi described the cycle in RBCs; Ronald Ross (1897) found the oocysts in the stomach wall of Anopheles and proved transmission by the mosquito (Nobel Prize 1902); Grassi (1898) completed the human cycle in Anopheles; Shortt and Garnham (1948) found the liver stage.

Diagnosis, treatment and control. Thick and thin blood smears stained by Giemsa or Leishman, or rapid antigen tests.

Drugs: quinine (from Cinchona bark), chloroquine, primaquine (kills hypnozoites and gametocytes — the "radical cure" of vivax), and artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for falciparum (artemisinin from Artemisia annua).

Control: insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, draining stagnant water, the larvivorous fish Gambusia, and the new vaccines (RTS,S and R21).

In Nepal most remaining cases are P. vivax in the Terai or imported, and the country is close to eliminating the disease.

Sickle-cell trait. Heterozygotes (HbA HbS) resist falciparum malaria: an infected RBC sickles and is removed by the spleen before the parasite completes its cycle — the classic example of balanced polymorphism.

Feature Anopheles (malaria) Culex (filaria, Japanese encephalitis)
Resting posture body at an angle (about 45°) to the surface body parallel to the surface, "hunch-backed"
Palps of the female as long as the proboscis much shorter than the proboscis
Eggs laid singly, each with lateral floats laid in rafts
Larva lies parallel to the water surface; no siphon hangs at an angle; breathes by a siphon
Wings spotted unspotted
How fast does a vivax infection grow?

Problem. A single infected RBC releases 16 merozoites at the end of each 48-hour cycle, and every merozoite infects a new RBC. Ignoring losses, how many RBCs are infected after three complete cycles?

Solution. The number multiplies by 16 each cycle: 16^3 = 4096 infected RBCs in 6 days. After six cycles (12 days) it would be 16^6 \approx 1.7 \times 10^7 — which is why symptoms appear about two weeks after a bite.

4.2 Earthworm (Pheretima): morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance

Position, habit and habitat

Pheretima posthuma (phylum Annelida, class Oligochaeta) is the common earthworm of Nepal's plains and valleys.

It lives in burrows in moist soil rich in humus, is nocturnal, fossorial and feeds on decaying leaves and organic matter swallowed with soil.

It comes out after heavy rain because water floods the burrows and it cannot breathe through a drowned skin.

Morphology

  • Body long, cylindrical, about 150 mm long and 3–5 mm thick, divided into about 100–120 segments (metameres); dark brown dorsally from the pigment porphyrin; a dark mid-dorsal line marks the dorsal blood vessel.
  • The prostomium — a fleshy lobe overhanging the mouth — is not a segment; it probes the soil. The first segment, bearing the mouth, is the peristomium.
  • Segments 14, 15 and 16 form the glandular clitellum (girdle). The body is thus pre-clitellar (1–13), clitellar (14–16) and post-clitellar (17 onwards).
  • Setae: S-shaped chitinous bristles in a ring round the middle of every segment (perichaetine), absent from the first segment, the last segment and the clitellum; they grip the soil in locomotion.
Aperture Number Position
Mouth 1 peristomium (segment 1)
Anus 1 last segment
Spermathecal pores 4 pairs ventro-lateral, in the grooves 5/6, 6/7, 7/8, 8/9
Female genital pore 1 mid-ventral, segment 14
Male genital pores 1 pair ventro-lateral, segment 18
Genital papillae 2 pairs segments 17 and 19
Dorsal pores 1 per groove mid-dorsal, from groove 12/13 backwards; release coelomic fluid to keep the skin moist
Nephridiopores very many all over the body except the first two segments

Body wall, coelom and locomotion

Body wall (outside in): cuticle → epidermis (columnar cells with gland cells) → circular muscles → longitudinal muscles → parietal peritoneum.

The coelom is a true schizocoel, divided by intersegmental septa and filled with milky, alkaline coelomic fluid with coelomocytes.

The fluid is the hydrostatic skeleton: circular muscles contract to make the front segments long and thin and push them forward; setae anchor them; longitudinal muscles then shorten the body and pull the rear up.

Chloragogen cells on the gut and blood vessels store glycogen and fat and remove nitrogenous waste (compared with the vertebrate liver).

Digestive system

Region Segments Notes
Mouth, buccal cavity 1–3 eversible
Pharynx 4 muscular, sucking; pharyngeal (salivary) glands secrete mucus and a protease
Oesophagus 5–7 narrow tube
Gizzard 8–9 thick, muscular, cuticle-lined; grinds soil and leaves
Stomach 9–14 glandular; calciferous glands secrete CaCO₃ that neutralises the humic acid of the humus
Intestine 15 to the last digestion and absorption; a pair of short conical intestinal caeca at segment 26; the typhlosole, a mid-dorsal fold, runs from segment 26 to all but the last 23–25 segments and increases the absorptive surface
Anus last worm castings leave here

Digestion is extracellular; the gut makes protease, amylase and lipase, and cellulose is broken down largely with the help of gut microbes.

Blood vascular system

  • Closed system; the blood is red because haemoglobin is dissolved in the plasma; the corpuscles are colourless, nucleated amoeboid cells.
  • Dorsal vessel: above the gut, contractile, with valves; blood flows forwards — the chief collecting vessel.
  • Ventral vessel: below the gut; blood flows backwards — the chief distributing vessel.
  • Four pairs of hearts: lateral hearts in segments 7 and 9 and latero-oesophageal hearts in segments 12 and 13, with valves, pumping from the dorsal to the ventral vessel.
  • Blood glands in segments 4, 5 and 6 make blood corpuscles and haemoglobin.

Respiration

There are no respiratory organs. Respiration is cutaneous: O₂ dissolves in the moist film of mucus and coelomic fluid on the skin and diffuses into a dense capillary network beneath the cuticle. A dry skin means death by suffocation.

Excretion

The excretory organs are coiled tubules, the nephridia — three kinds in Pheretima.

Nephridia Position Opening Nephrostome
Septal both faces of each septum from segment 15 to the last into the intestine (enteronephric) present
Integumentary inner surface of the body wall from segment 3 to the last; very many on the clitellum outside by nephridiopores (exonephric) absent
Pharyngeal three paired tufts in segments 4, 5 and 6 into the buccal cavity and pharynx (enteronephric) absent

The worm excretes ammonia in wet soil and more urea when dry (ammonotelic → ureotelic). Enteronephric nephridia send the urine into the gut, where water is reabsorbed — a water-saving adaptation.

Nervous system and sense organs

A pair of cerebral (supra-pharyngeal) ganglia — the "brain" — lies above the pharynx in segment 3; circum-pharyngeal connectives join them to the sub-pharyngeal ganglia in segment 4, forming a nerve ring; from these the ventral nerve cord — double but fused, solid, with a ganglion in every segment — runs to the hind end.

There are no eyes: photoreceptor cells (mostly on the prostomium and dorsal surface) sense light, and epidermal receptors sense touch and chemicals; chemoreceptors in the buccal cavity taste food.

Reproduction and development

The earthworm is hermaphrodite (monoecious) but protandrous — the testes mature before the ovaries — so cross-fertilisation is the rule.

Male organs Segments Female organs Segments
2 pairs of testes in testis sacs 10 and 11 1 pair of ovaries (on septum 12/13) 13
2 pairs of seminal vesicles 11 and 12 ovarian funnels and oviducts 13–14
vasa deferentia 10 to 18 single female genital pore 14
1 pair of large prostate glands about 16/17 to 20/21 4 pairs of spermathecae 6, 7, 8, 9
male genital pores 18
2 pairs of accessory glands (open on the genital papillae) 17 and 19

Copulation (on damp nights): two worms join ventral surfaces head-to-tail and exchange sperm, which are stored in each other's spermathecae.

Later the clitellum secretes a cocoon; as the worm wriggles backwards out of it, the cocoon collects ova at segment 14 and sperm from the spermathecae at segments 6–9.

Fertilisation therefore takes place in the cocoon, outside the body (external). The cocoon is left in the soil; after about three weeks it releases 2–20 young worms (on average about four).

Development is direct — no larva. Earthworms also regenerate lost parts.

Two marks that are regularly lost

(1) Hermaphrodite does not mean self-fertilising — Pheretima is protandrous and cross-fertilising. (2) Sperm pass from worm to worm, but fertilisation is external, inside the cocoon. And remember the single female pore (14) lies in front of the paired male pores (18).

Economic importance

  • Farmer's friend: burrows aerate and drain the soil and let roots penetrate; worms bring subsoil up and bury organic matter (Darwin, The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, 1881).
  • Castings are rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and humus.
  • Vermicomposting (vermiculture) turns farm and kitchen waste into manure; Eisenia fetida (red wiggler) and Perionyx excavatus are the usual species.
  • Worms are fish bait, a protein-rich feed for poultry and fish, and are used in traditional medicine.
  • Harmful: casts spoil lawns and seedbeds; earthworms are intermediate hosts of the poultry gapeworm Syngamus and the lungworm of pigs; they host the gregarine Monocystis in their seminal vesicles.
Earthworm segment numbers

"3-4 brain, 4 pharynx, 5-7 gullet, 8-9 gizzard, 9-14 stomach"; then the reproductive run "6-9 spermathecae, 10-11 testes, 13 ovaries, 14 female, 17 and 19 papillae, 18 male"; hearts 7, 9, 12, 13; caeca and typhlosole from 26.

4.3 Frog (Rana): morphology, body systems and physiology

Position, habit and habitat

Rana tigrina (now Hoplobatrachus tigerinus, the Indian bullfrog; Chordata → Vertebrata → Amphibia → order Anura) lives in and near ponds, ditches and paddy fields of the Terai and valleys.

It is amphibious, carnivorous (insects, worms, snails) and poikilothermic (cold-blooded): it escapes winter cold by hibernation (winter sleep) and summer heat and drought by aestivation (summer sleep), buried in mud and breathing through its skin.

It changes skin colour with its surroundings by means of chromatophores (camouflage).

Morphology

  • Body of head and trunk; no neck and no tail in the adult.
  • Skin smooth, moist, slimy, scaleless, loosely attached, rich in mucous glands and capillaries. The frog never drinks water — it absorbs water through the skin.
  • Head: wide mouth, a pair of external nares, bulging eyes with a fixed upper lid, a movable lower lid and a transparent nictitating membrane that protects the eye under water; behind each eye a circular tympanum (ear drum) — there is no external ear.
  • Forelimbs short, with 4 digits; hindlimbs long and muscular, with 5 webbed toes for leaping and swimming.
  • A single cloacal aperture at the hind end passes faeces, urine and gametes.
  • Sexual dimorphism: the male has a pair of vocal sacs (croaking) and a nuptial (copulatory) pad on the first digit of each forelimb; the female has neither.

Skeleton (the facts that are asked)

Part Feature
Skull dicondylic (two occipital condyles); teeth on the upper jaw (maxillary) and palate (vomerine); lower jaw toothless
Vertebral column only 9 vertebrae + a rod-like urostyle; the first (atlas) has no transverse processes
Ribs absent
Limb bones radio-ulna and tibio-fibula fused; long ankle (tarsal) bones for leaping
Calcified cartilage suprascapula

Digestive system

Mouth → buccal cavity with maxillary and vomerine teeth (they grip prey, they do not chew; teeth homodont, acrodont and replaced throughout life) and a sticky bilobed tongue attached in front and free behind, flicked out to catch insects → pharynx → short oesophagus → stomach (cardiac and pyloric parts; HCl and pepsin) → duodenum → coiled ileum with villi (digestion completed, absorption) → rectum → cloaca.

The liver (three lobes) secretes bile, stored in the gall bladder; the pancreas lies between stomach and duodenum; the bile duct and pancreatic duct join to form the common bile duct, opening into the duodenum.

The adult's gut is short (carnivore); the herbivorous tadpole's is long and coiled.

Respiration

The frog breathes in three ways:

Mode Organ When
Cutaneous moist, thin, vascular skin always — in water, on land and the only route during hibernation and aestivation; gets rid of most of the CO₂
Buccopharyngeal moist lining of the buccal cavity at rest on land, mouth shut (the throat flutters)
Pulmonary a pair of thin, elastic, sac-like lungs with internal septa forming alveoli when active on land

Pathway of air: external nares → nasal chambers → internal nares → buccal cavity → glottis → laryngo-tracheal chamber → lungs.

With no diaphragm and no ribs, the frog fills its lungs by a buccal force pump (positive pressure): with the glottis shut it lowers the buccal floor and draws air in through the nostrils; it then closes the nostrils, opens the glottis and raises the buccal floor, forcing the air into the lungs.

Expiration is by elastic recoil and pressure of the body wall. The tadpole breathes by gills.

Blood vascular system

  • Closed, with a three-chambered heart — two atria (auricles) and one ventricle — in a pericardium, plus two accessory chambers.
  • Sinus venosus (dorsal, thin-walled) receives deoxygenated blood from two precavals and one postcaval and opens into the right atrium; it is the pacemaker — the heartbeat starts here.
  • Pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium.
  • Both atria empty into the single ventricle, whose spongy wall (trabeculae) limits mixing.
  • Truncus (conus) arteriosus leaves the ventricle on the ventral side; its spiral valve directs the most deoxygenated blood into the pulmocutaneous arch (lungs and skin), mixed blood into the systemic arch (body) and the best-oxygenated blood into the carotid arch (head).
  • Circulation is double but incomplete (some mixing). Hepatic portal and renal portal systems are present; the lymphatic system has lymph hearts.
  • Blood: plasma with nucleated, oval, biconvex RBCs, WBCs and spindle-shaped thrombocytes.

Excretion and osmoregulation

A pair of dark-red mesonephric kidneys lies against the dorsal body wall, each with a yellow adrenal gland on its ventral face.

Ureters open into the cloaca; in the male the ureter also carries sperm and is called the urinogenital duct, while in the female the ureter and oviduct open separately into the cloaca.

The thin-walled, bilobed urinary bladder opens ventrally into the cloaca, not into the ureters, and lets water be reabsorbed on land. The adult is ureotelic (urea); the aquatic tadpole is ammonotelic (ammonia).

Nervous system, sense organs and endocrine glands

CNS: brain in the cranium and spinal cord in the neural canal, wrapped in meninges. PNS: 10 pairs of cranial nerves and 10 pairs of spinal nerves; an autonomic system as well.

Brain region Parts Job
Forebrain a pair of olfactory lobes, a pair of cerebral hemispheres, the diencephalon with the pineal body above and the optic chiasma, infundibulum and pituitary below smell, voluntary activity, hormone control
Midbrain a pair of large optic lobes vision
Hindbrain a small cerebellum and the medulla oblongata balance; breathing, heartbeat and other reflex centres

Sense organs: eyes (with nictitating membrane), ears (tympanum, a middle ear with one ossicle, the columella, and an internal ear for hearing and balance), nasal epithelium (smell), taste buds and skin papillae (touch).

The tadpole has a lateral line system, lost at metamorphosis.

Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads. Thyroxine from the thyroid controls metamorphosis.

Reproduction and development

The frog is dioecious; fertilisation is external; development is indirect through a tadpole larva.

Male Female
a pair of yellowish oval testes, attached to the kidneys and body wall by the mesorchium a pair of lobed ovaries near the kidneys, attached by the mesovarium, not connected to the kidneys
10–12 vasa efferentia carry sperm into the kidney → Bidder's canal → urinogenital duct (ureter) → a dilated seminal vesicle → cloaca ova are shed into the coelom and enter the funnel-shaped ostium of the long coiled oviduct; its hind end, the ovisac, opens into the cloaca
finger-like fat bodies store food for the breeding season lays 2500–3000 eggs at a time in jelly-coated masses

Breeding follows the first monsoon rains. In amplexus the male clasps the female with the nuptial pads; she sheds eggs into the water and he sheds sperm over them at once.

Amplexus is not copulation — fertilisation is external. The egg hatches into a tadpole: aquatic, herbivorous, with horny jaws, a long coiled gut, a tail with fins, external then internal gills, a two-chambered heart, a lateral line, no limbs, and ammonotelic.

Metamorphosis, controlled by thyroxine (which needs iodine), turns the tadpole into a frog.

Progressive changes: hindlimbs appear first, then forelimbs; lungs develop; heart becomes three-chambered; eyelids and tympanum form; the gut shortens; excretion becomes ureotelic.

Retrogressive changes: the tail is resorbed (by lysosomal enzymes), gills, horny jaws and lateral line disappear.

Tadpoles given thyroxine metamorphose early into tiny frogs; tadpoles deprived of thyroid hormone or iodine stay as giant tadpoles.

Frog traps
  • The heartbeat starts in the sinus venosus, not in the SA node (the frog has none).
  • The frog's RBCs are nucleated and oval, unlike the mammal's.
  • The male's ureter carries urine and sperm; the female's oviduct is separate from the ureter.
  • The urinary bladder opens into the cloaca, not into the ureters.
  • Only the upper jaw carries teeth; the lower jaw is toothless.
Three columns for every frog question

Most frog questions are answered by placing the fact in one of three columns: tadpole (gills, two-chambered heart, ammonia, herbivore, lateral line) → metamorphosis (thyroxine) → adult (lungs and skin, three-chambered heart, urea, carnivore).

Timing erythrocytic schizogony and fever paroxysms in malaria

Problem. A patient presents with classic paroxysms of chill, high fever, and sweating recurring every 48 hours, and peripheral blood smear shows enlarged, stippled RBCs with Schüffner's dots.

Identify the Plasmodium species and explain why the fever recurs every 48 hours.

Solution. A 48-hour benign tertian cycle with enlarged host RBCs bearing Schüffner's dots identifies Plasmodium vivax. Fever spikes when erythrocytic schizonts rupture synchronously every 48 hours, releasing merozoites and the pyrogenic toxin haemozoin into the plasma.

Segmental landmarks of Pheretima posthuma

Problem. Give the exact segment numbers in Pheretima posthuma for(a) the gizzard,(b) the clitellum,(c) the single female genital pore,(d) the paired male genital pores, and(e) the four pairs of spermathecal apertures.

Solution.(a) Gizzard: 8 (or 8–9);(b) clitellum: 14, 15, and 16;(c) female pore: mid-ventral on 14;(d) male pores: ventro-lateral on 18;(e) spermathecal pores: intersegmental grooves 5/6, 6/7, 7/8, and 8/9.

Chapter summary

  • Plasmodium (Sporozoa) is a digenetic intracellular parasite: asexual schizogony in man (intermediate host) — liver cells, then the 48-hour Golgi cycle in RBCs — and sexual phase in the female Anopheles (definitive host) — gametes, zygote, ookinete, oocyst, sporozoites in the salivary glands.
  • The sporozoite infects man and the gametocyte infects the mosquito; the zygote is the only diploid stage; the fever follows the synchronous bursting of RBCs and the release of haemozoin.
  • P. vivax (benign tertian, relapses from hypnozoites, commonest in Nepal), P. falciparum (malignant tertian, cerebral malaria), P. malariae (quartan, 72 h) and P. ovale (ovale tertian).
  • Pheretima posthuma: about 100–120 segments; prostomium; clitellum 14–16; perichaetine setae; female pore 14, male pores 18, papillae 17 and 19, spermathecal pores 5/6–8/9.
  • Earthworm gut: pharynx 4, gizzard 8–9, stomach 9–14 with calciferous glands, caeca and typhlosole from 26; closed circulation with Hb in plasma and four pairs of hearts (7, 9, 12, 13); cutaneous respiration; septal, integumentary and pharyngeal nephridia.
  • The earthworm is a protandrous hermaphrodite: testes 10–11, ovaries 13, spermathecae 6–9; cross-fertilisation, fertilisation in the cocoon, direct development; it is the farmer's friend and the basis of vermicomposting.
  • The frog (Rana tigrina) breathes by skin, buccopharynx and lungs (buccal force pump); its three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and spiral valve gives a double but incomplete circulation; RBCs are nucleated.
  • The frog is ureotelic with mesonephric kidneys; the male's ureter is a urinogenital duct; it has 10 pairs of cranial nerves, 9 vertebrae and a urostyle; fertilisation is external after amplexus, and thyroxine drives metamorphosis of the tadpole.

Model answer D1: Life cycle of Plasmodium vivax and types of malaria (10 marks)

Introduction. Plasmodium is a unicellular sporozoan parasite of man that causes malaria. It is digenetic: it lives in two hosts. Man is the intermediate host (asexual cycle, schizogony) and the female Anopheles mosquito is the definitive host (sexual cycle, sporogony).

Life cycle in man.

  1. Infection: an infected female Anopheles injects sporozoites with saliva when she bites.
  2. Pre-erythrocytic (liver) cycle: the sporozoites enter liver cells and divide by schizogony for about 7–10 days, giving thousands of merozoites.
  3. Erythrocytic cycle: merozoites enter red blood cells and grow into a ring-shaped trophozoite, then an amoeboid form, then a schizont, which divides into 12–24 merozoites.
  4. Release: the red cell bursts, releasing merozoites, haemozoin and toxins. This produces the typical chill, fever and sweating every 48 hours in P. vivax.
  5. Gametocytes: after several cycles some merozoites form micro- and macrogametocytes, which wait in the blood.
  6. Relapse: in P. vivax and P. ovale dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) may start the cycle again after months.

Life cycle in the mosquito.

  1. A female Anopheles sucks blood and takes in the gametocytes.
  2. In her gut the gametes fuse (fertilisation) to form a zygote, which becomes a motile ookinete.
  3. It enters the stomach wall and forms an oocyst, which divides by sporogony into thousands of sporozoites.
  4. They move to the salivary glands, ready to infect the next person (7–10 days).

Types of malaria.

Species Disease Fever repeats Note
P. vivax Benign tertian Every 48 h Common in the Nepali Terai; relapses
P. falciparum Malignant tertian 36–48 h, irregular Most dangerous; cerebral malaria
P. malariae Quartan Every 72 h Mild, long-lasting
P. ovale Mild tertian Every 48 h Rare

Control and prevention. Drain stagnant water, use larvicides and insecticide-treated bed nets, spray houses, take antimalarial drugs (chloroquine, artemisinin combination therapy), and diagnose early by blood smear or rapid test.

Nepal's malaria cases are now mostly in the Terai and border districts.

Conclusion. The cycle needs both man and the female Anopheles, so breaking the contact between them is the best way to control malaria.

Model answer D2: Earthworm (Pheretima) (10 marks)

Introduction. Earthworms are annelids of the class Oligochaeta that live in burrows in moist, humus-rich soil and come out at night. Aristotle called them the "intestines of the soil".

External features. The body is long, cylindrical and made of 100–120 segments (metameres) with no head or appendages. The first segment has the prostomium (a sensory lobe over the mouth).

Segments 14–16 form the clitellum (a glandular ring that makes the cocoon). Each segment has a ring of S-shaped setae for locomotion.

The openings include the female genital pore (segment 14), a pair of male pores (segment 18) and spermathecal pores (between segments 5 and 9).

Body systems.

  1. Digestive: mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx (with salivary glands) → oesophagus (calciferous glands neutralise the humic acid) → gizzard (grinds soil) → stomach → intestine with a fold called the typhlosole that increases the absorbing surface → anus.
  2. Circulatory: closed; dorsal and ventral vessels joined by four pairs of hearts; the red pigment haemoglobin is dissolved in the plasma.
  3. Respiratory: exchange of gases through the moist skin (cutaneous respiration).
  4. Excretory: tiny coiled tubes, the nephridia (septal, pharyngeal and integumentary), remove urea and ammonia.
  5. Nervous: a nerve ring around the pharynx with cerebral ganglia, and a double ventral nerve cord with a ganglion in each segment; sense organs include touch and light cells.
  6. Reproductive: hermaphrodite but cross-fertilisation occurs, since the male and female organs mature at different times (protandry). Sperms are exchanged during mating, and the clitellum forms a cocoon that holds fertilised eggs. Development is direct.

Economic importance.

Useful Harmful or limit
Burrowing aerates and drains soil Some may carry parasite eggs
Casts add nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium Can damage seedlings in nurseries
Used in vermicompost units in Nepal Sensitive to chemicals and drought
Fish bait –

Conclusion. The earthworm is a "farmer's friend" whose segmented body, closed circulation and nephridia are good examples of the annelid plan.

Model answer D3: The frog (Rana tigrina) (10 marks)

Introduction. The common Indian bullfrog, Rana tigrina, is an amphibian that lives near ponds and paddy fields and is active in the monsoon.

External features. The body has a head and trunk with no neck. The skin is smooth, moist and mucous, often olive-green with dark patches. The eyes have nictitating membranes, and behind them is the tympanum.

The forelimb has 4 digits and the webbed hind limb has 5 for jumping and swimming. The male has vocal sacs and nuptial pads.

Body systems.

  1. Digestive: a wide mouth with a bifid, sticky tongue, small maxillary and vomerine teeth; then oesophagus, stomach, intestine, rectum and cloaca. The liver (with bile) and pancreas help. The frog is carnivorous.
  2. Respiratory: three modes — cutaneous (skin, in water and in hibernation), buccopharyngeal (mouth lining) and pulmonary (a pair of simple lungs on land).
  3. Circulatory: three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) with a sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus. Blood is partly mixed. The red cells are oval and nucleated. There are hepatic portal and renal portal systems.
  4. Excretory: a pair of kidneys (mesonephric) with ureters to the cloaca and a urinary bladder. Frogs excrete urea (ureotelic).
  5. Nervous: brain (fore-, mid- and hind-brain) in the cranium, with 10 pairs of cranial nerves and a spinal cord with 10 pairs of spinal nerves.
  6. Reproduction: sexes are separate. External fertilisation takes place in water, eggs hatch into tadpoles that undergo metamorphosis controlled by thyroxine.
Feature Earthworm Frog
Phylum Annelida Chordata
Heart Four pairs of hearts, closed Three-chambered
Respiration Skin Skin, mouth, lungs
Excretion Nephridia Kidneys
Sexes Hermaphrodite Separate

Conclusion. The frog's three ways of breathing and its tadpole stage show its position between water and land life.
